Original papers in Experimental Economics are, on average, about 28 pages long, while original papers in Psychology are only about 11 pages — roughly 2.5 times shorter.

**Hypothesis (answer to the question):** Based on the replication-projects dataset, original papers in Experimental Economics (project = ee) average 28.0 pages, whereas original papers in Psychology (project = rpp) average 11.2 pages. This large gap (16.8 pages, ratio ≈ 2.5×) likely reflects journal-format differences: the Experimental Economics originals were published in top economics journals (American Economic Review, Quarterly Journal of Economics) with long article formats, while the Psychology originals come from Psychological Science and JEP:LMC, which include many short report-format articles.

**Results (computed from `length` column, one row per unique original paper):**

| Group | N | Mean | Median | SD | Range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Experimental Economics (ee) | 18 | 28.00 | 28 | 7.37 | 16–45 |
| Psychology (rpp) | 97 | 11.22 | 9 | 6.30 | 1–31 |

**Required caveats:**
1. **Skew and format comparability:** the rpp distribution is right-skewed (median 9 vs mean 11.2) and includes very short articles of 1–5 pages (short report format in Psychological Science). Page counts across different journal formats are only an approximate like-for-like comparison; the ee papers (16–45 pages, AER/QJE) are uniformly long-article format.
2. **Sample sizes:** the ee mean rests on only 18 papers, the rpp mean on 97 papers.

**Workflow:** loaded the study-data CSV (927 rows × 57 cols); verified ee and rpp each have exactly one row per unique id (no double-counting; ml1/ml3 excluded as separate projects per approved plan); confirmed `length` is clean int64 with zero missing values in both groups; computed mean/median/SD/range per group. The replication-success CSV was not used (it contains no `length` column).
